newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil rains wash out early coffee quality hopes.
newsitem.headline: Brazil rains wash out early coffee quality hopes.

text.p: Recent rains in key Brazilian coffee areas have hit coffee quality and may disrupt the flow of coffee to the market through July, traders and producers said.

In a daily report, Santos brokers Wolthers and Associates said that the rains, mainly in the Cerrado and southern regions of Minas Gerais state, had delayed the harvest and was said by some producers to have already spoiled the cup quality.
"The main concern is about the delay, once many producers sold the coffee to be delivered in July and some of them said they will not be able to honor commitments," the report said.
Manoel Bertone, vice-president of the growers' National Coffee Council, said he thought there should be no problem meeting commitments as any pre-sales were for small quantities.
"But exports may be lower than expected because there will be less available," Bertone said.

The 1997/98 Brazilian harvest had got off to a good start this year with producers at the end of May commenting on the excellent quality of early arrivals following a long dry spell which in some places began mid-March.

But rains in the last two weeks have come at just the wrong time for picking the current harvest although at the right time for bringing much needed moisture to the ground, benefiting the 1998/99 crop.

Around 10 to 15 percent of the crop has fallen to the ground due to rains in the south of Minas Gerais and the Zona da Mata region, said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Association.
In Garca, southwest Sao Paulo state, the percentage is even higher, according to Bertone, who is also president of the local cooperative.
The coffee should dry out after three days of sunshine and while no losses are expected in terms of quantity, quality will be hit, Bertone said.

In the Cerrado area of Minas Gerais, only around 15 percent of the harvest had so far been picked because of the rains, said Aguinaldo Lima, president of the Cerrado coffee growers association Caccer.
Normally 30 percent of the crop would have been brought in by the end of June, he added.
"I have been in here for 15 years and I have never seen so much rain and so much cold," Lima said.
With the rains there were obviously concerns about quality but there would only be real damage if the rains continued, he said.
In terms of quantity, coffee exports in July are expected to reach around one million bags, limited by the problems with the harvest, growers and traders said.
Export registrations for July to June 13 were said to be just over the one million bag mark and producers did not expect the supply of coffee to allow for higher shipments.
"If we make one million bags in exports, then I think it will be very good," Bertone said.
In July 1996, exports reached 1.16 million bags while in the same month in 1995, shipments totaled 955,436 bags.
One other phenomenon caused by the rains is that in some areas of southern Minas Gerais there has already been a flowering for the 1998/99 crop, something which normally only begins around September.

While this does not necessarily mean any impact on the crop, producers are concerned about anything which may reduce the 1998/99 harvest, expected to mark a resounding recovery from the weather problems of 1994.

"God willing and no weather problems, we could have a beautiful crop next year of 35 million bags," said Joaquim Libanio Leite, export director at Cooxupe cooperative in Guaxupe, a key cooperative and exporter.
((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
